title: Draft-and-Continue Self-Consistency: An Empirical Study of Two-Stage Branch Budgeting for LLM Reasoning

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to investigate whether adaptive compute allocation to promising branches can improve self-consistency efficiency. Paper [2] ("Reliability-Aware Adaptive Self-Consistency for Efficient Sampling in LLM Reasoning") shares a substantively equivalent purpose, as it also aims to improve self-consistency efficiency through adaptive sampling strategies. Specifically, it reframes adaptive sampling to reduce unnecessary computation, which aligns with the goal of optimizing compute allocation for efficiency.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, Draft-and-Continue Self-Consistency (DCS), involves a two-stage process: sampling multiple short drafts, extracting interim answers, selecting high-vote branches, and continuing them with a hedge allocation strategy. Paper [12] ("SelfBudgeter: Adaptive Token Allocation for Efficient LLM Reasoning") contains a substantively equivalent mechanism. SelfBudgeter uses adaptive token allocation strategies to optimize reasoning efficiency, which parallels the idea of selectively allocating compute resources to promising branches. Additionally, paper [6] ("On the Convergence of Optimal Computing Budget Allocation Algorithms") discusses optimal allocation of resources across competing designs, which is conceptually equivalent to the hedge allocation strategy in DCS.

### Evaluation
The evaluation design involves a two-stage method with a fixed token budget per problem and specific sampling parameters (temperature 0.8, top-p 0.95). Paper [1] ("Two-Round Voting: Improving Self-Consistency by Recycling Low-Vote Reasoning Evidence") uses a similar two-stage self-consistency framework, validating its method with a fixed sampling budget and aggregation strategy. Paper [4] ("Confidence-Guided Early Stopping for Efficient and Accurate Self-Consistency") also employs a two-stage self-consistency evaluation design, with adaptive stopping rules based on confidence signals. Both papers share the same evaluation design family, even though the specific benchmarks and parameters differ.

### Domain
The domain is LLM mathematical reasoning and test-time compute allocation. Paper [1] ("Two-Round Voting: Improving Self-Consistency by Recycling Low-Vote Reasoning Evidence") and paper [4] ("Confidence-Guided Early Stopping for Efficient and Accurate Self-Consistency") both operate in the same general application area of LLM reasoning tasks, including mathematical reasoning. While the specific sub-problems or datasets may differ, the domain is covered.

**PURPOSE: Investigate whether adaptive compute allocation to promising branches can improve self-consistency efficiency.**

Papers [1], [2], [4], [23] all address improving self-consistency efficiency through adaptive/selective sampling. Paper [2] (ReASC) explicitly addresses "adjusting the sampling budget" for self-consistency. Paper [4] (CGES) addresses "adaptively halts sampling" for self-consistency efficiency. Paper [1] recycles low-vote chains to improve SC efficiency. Paper [23] (BEACON) addresses "deciding when to stop generating new samples to balance accuracy gains against efficiency." All of these share the same objective: improve self-consistency efficiency through adaptive compute allocation. The purpose is covered.

**MECHANISM: Draft-and-Continue Self-Consistency (DCS): two-stage process where short drafts are sampled, vote histogram built, top-k branches selected and continued, with hedge allocation reserving a slot for second-place answer.**

The specific mechanism involves: (1) generating short drafts, (2) building a vote histogram, (3) selecting top-k branches to continue, (4) hedge allocation. Paper [1] recycles low-vote reasoning evidence in a two-round voting scheme — it uses vote information to guide further processing of chains, but focuses on recycling low-vote chains rather than continuing high-vote ones. Paper [2] uses evidence sufficiency rather than vote counts. Paper [4] uses Bayesian posteriors for early stopping. None of these prior papers implement the specific "draft short → vote histogram → select top-k → continue those specific branches" pipeline. The hedge allocation (reserving a slot for second-place) is also not described in any prior paper. This mechanism appears genuinely absent from prior work.

**EVALUATION: Two-stage method with ~10,240 token budget per problem; sampling temperature 0.8, top-p 0.95.**

The evaluation description here is essentially a description of the method's configuration rather than a distinct evaluation design. Looking at what evaluation design is used: it appears to be standard LLM mathematical reasoning benchmarks with accuracy metrics, compared against baselines at iso-compute budgets. Papers [1], [2], [4], [12], [23] all evaluate self-consistency methods on mathematical reasoning benchmarks using accuracy metrics and token/sample budget comparisons. The evaluation design (accuracy on math benchmarks, iso-compute comparison) is covered by these prior papers. The specific token budget numbers are parameters, not a new design.

**DOMAIN: LLM mathematical reasoning / test-time compute allocation.**

Papers [1], [2], [4], [12], [14], [23] all operate in LLM mathematical reasoning with test-time compute allocation. This domain is clearly covered.

The contribution's purpose is to explain the negative result and derive a general condition under which two-stage budgeting fails. Paper [4] ("Two-stage Budgeting with Bounded Rationality") constructs a unifying theory of two-stage budgeting and bounded rationality, addressing behavioral wedges between first-stage and second-stage budgets. While [4] focuses on mental accounting and rational inattention, it does not establish the specific failure condition or negative result described in the contribution. No other paper explicitly reports or establishes the same empirical relationship or failure condition. Thus, the purpose is **not covered**.

The contribution uses diagnostic analysis of draft completion rate and fallback fraction, arguing that effectiveness depends on the relationship between draft length and problem complexity. Paper [10] ("Draft Model Knows When to Stop") discusses the discrepancy between fixed draft lengths and problem complexity in speculative decoding, analyzing how draft length impacts performance. Similarly, paper [14] ("PACER: Blockwise Pre-verification for Speculative Decoding with Adaptive Length") explores adaptive draft lengths and their relationship to decoding efficiency. Both papers employ substantively equivalent mechanisms of analyzing draft length and its interaction with task complexity. Thus, the mechanism is **covered**.

Paper [6] ("Reliability-Aware Adaptive Self-Consistency") also evaluates adaptive self-consistency methods using comparable metrics. These prior papers use the same evaluation design (benchmark family and metric semantics), even though the specific objects differ. Thus, the evaluation is **covered**.

**PURPOSE: Explain the negative result and derive a general condition under which two-stage budgeting fails.**

The purpose is specifically to explain *why* a two-stage budgeting approach (DCS) fails — diagnosing the failure mode and deriving a general condition. Paper [22] "When Does Confidence-Based Cascade Deferral Suffice?" asks exactly when a cascade/deferral strategy works or fails, deriving conditions for sufficiency. This is structurally equivalent: both seek to characterize the failure conditions of a staged/cascade inference strategy. Paper [5] (RASC/Dynamic Self-Consistency) addresses limitations of self-consistency but doesn't derive failure conditions for two-stage budgeting specifically. No other paper establishes the same empirical relationship (two-stage budgeting degenerates when draft completion rate is too high).

Paper [22] is the closest match — it derives conditions under which confidence-based cascade deferral suffices/fails, which is the same class of purpose (characterizing when a staged inference strategy degenerates).

**MECHANISM: Diagnostic analysis of draft completion rate and fallback fraction; argue effectiveness depends on relationship between draft length and problem complexity.**

The mechanism is a diagnostic analysis measuring completion rates and fallback fractions to argue that a two-stage system degenerates when drafts almost always complete. Paper [10] "Draft Model Knows When to Stop" discusses how oracle draft length varies with problem complexity and that fixed-length policies fail under complex reasoning — this touches on the relationship between draft length and complexity. Paper [14] (PACER) also notes "optimal draft length varies significantly across different decoding steps." However, these are in speculative decoding, not self-consistency. The diagnostic framing (measuring completion rate and fallback fraction as the analytical primitive to explain system degeneration) is not explicitly present in any prior paper. Paper [22] uses theoretical analysis rather than this specific diagnostic. No prior paper uses completion-rate + fallback-fraction diagnostics to explain two-stage self-consistency failure.

**EVALUATION: ~96.3% drafts complete within T_draft=1024, fallback only 3.73%, DCS degenerates; CGES-LNS Pareto-dominates DCS (identical accuracy, 52% fewer tokens, 2.48 vs ~10 calls).**

The evaluation design involves: (1) measuring fallback/completion rates as diagnostic statistics, (2) Pareto-dominance comparison on accuracy vs. token-cost tradeoff, (3) comparing self-consistency variants on reasoning benchmarks. Paper [1] (CGES) uses accuracy vs. number-of-calls comparisons for self-consistency variants — same metric semantics (accuracy, call count, token efficiency). Paper [5] (RASC) also compares self-consistency methods on accuracy and sampling efficiency. The Pareto-dominance framing and token-count comparison appear in [1] and [6]. The evaluation design (compare SC variants on accuracy + cost metrics on reasoning benchmarks) is covered by [1], [5], [6].

**DOMAIN: Efficiency analysis of self-consistency variants.**

Papers [1], [5], [6], [17] all work in the domain of efficient self-consistency for LLM reasoning. This is clearly covered.
